content:
A common claim says that Jewish rabbis met at Jamnia, a town near the coast, about the year AD 90 and closed the Hebrew Bible. Writers on both sides of the Muslim and Christian conversation repeat it, to say the Hebrew scriptures were fixed at a known date or by a late human committee.

The claim has a source, and the source says less than the claim does. The six facts below set out what the record contains, what a nineteenth-century historian of the canon made of it, and why many scholars of the Hebrew Bible have since dropped the picture of a closing council.

In 1877 Samuel Davidson wrote in his history of the canon: "The canon was virtually settled at Jamnia".[1] That sentence passed into many handbooks.

Read it closely. The word is "virtually". Davidson never claimed a vote on a list or a finished matter.

The rabbinic record of Jamnia, and of an earlier debate at Jerusalem about AD 65, concerns whether certain books were sacred enough to "pollute the hands".[2] The books under discussion were Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs. Davidson adds doubts about Esther, Proverbs and Ezekiel.

People were already reading these books. The debate asked about their standing, and no list of the books of the Bible came out of it.

A few pages after the sentence above, Davidson wrote: "The canon was not really settled for all time by a synodical gathering at Jamnia".[3] The same book that says virtually settled also says not settled for all time.

His evidence is plain. Sirach and Baruch, books outside the Hebrew list, were still treated with canonical regard in the third and fourth centuries.

In 1964 Jack P. Lewis argued that the sources describe a school of scholars at Jabneh, and that the idea of a council with power to close the canon is a modern construction.[4] Many scholars of the Hebrew Bible now accept the main point.

I think it is fair to say the older picture has few defenders. The debate continues over what the rabbis of that period did decide about particular books, and over when the third division of the Hebrew Bible took its final shape.

The prologue to Sirach, written about 130 BC, names "the law and the prophets" and "the rest of the books" without giving a list. Josephus, writing in the first century AD, counts twenty-two books "which are justly believed to be divine".[5]

Davidson called Josephus an authority of small weight and his claim a Pharisaic view "probably expressed in exaggerated terms". Even so, the two texts show a Law and Prophets that were fixed in practice well before Jamnia, and a third group whose edges stayed open.

Other scholars hold that the Hebrew list was closed before the first century AD, and that Jamnia only confirmed the doubtful books.[6] Both positions agree that no single act at Jamnia closed the canon.

For a reader who asks which Hebrew scriptures existed in the time of the prophets and of Jesus, peace be upon him, the careful answer names a Law and Prophets that were settled early and a set of Writings that took longer.[7]

The bottom line

Jamnia was a debate in a school about two or three books, recorded generations later, with no council and no list.

A claim that depends on the Hebrew Bible closing at a known date in AD 90 has to find another date, or another argument.

Notes

  1. Samuel Davidson, The Canon of the Bible: Its Formation, History, and Fluctuations (New York: Peter Eckler, 1877), p. 32.
  2. Samuel Davidson, The Canon of the Bible: Its Formation, History, and Fluctuations (New York: Peter Eckler, 1877), pp. 31 to 32. The Mishnah tractate Yadayim 3:5 records the discussion about whether Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs make the hands unclean.
  3. Davidson, Canon, p. 35.
  4. Jack P. Lewis, "What Do We Mean by Jabneh?", Journal of Bible and Religion 32 (1964), pp. 125 to 132; John Barton, Holy Writings, Sacred Text: The Canon in Early Christianity (Louisville: Westminster John Knox, 1997).
  5. Davidson, Canon, pp. 27 to 29 and 39. Josephus, Against Apion 1.37 to 42.
  6. Sid Z. Leiman, The Canonization of Hebrew Scripture: The Talmudic and Midrashic Evidence (Hamden: Archon Books, 1976); Roger T. Beckwith, The Old Testament Canon of the New Testament Church (Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1985).
  7. See the site's articles on the Septuagint and on the oldest Bible codices.
